title: The seed of the banyan
hook: a father has his son break open a banyan seed and find nothing, and the whole year comes down to one line
carry: tat tvam asi: that you are
tomorrow: why does the greatest war story start with snakes?

segments.voice: Yesterday: jnana, and the tenth man. The Self is known, not earned. Today, the last day of year two.

A son comes home after twelve years of study, sure he knows everything. His father, Uddalaka, isn't so sure. He points at a great banyan tree. Bring me one of its fruits. Here it is, sir. Break it. It's broken, sir. What do you see? Tiny seeds. Break one of those. Done. What do you see now? The son, Shvetaketu, looks closely. Nothing at all, sir.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.` → `NOTHING AT ALL, SIR.`

segments.voice: This is the Chandogya Upanishad, where year two began. Uddalaka says: that fine essence you can't see, my son, out of it this whole great banyan stands. That finest essence is the Self of all that is. That is the real. And you are that, Shvetaketu. Tat tvam asi. It's counted among the great sayings of the Upanishads, the mahavakyas, and here's the teaching plainly: the deepest Self in you, atman, and Brahman, the reality behind everything, are not strangers. What you can't see holds up what you can. That line sits under this whole year. You heard Uddalaka again with salt dissolved in water: you can't see it, but every sip tastes of it. You heard Gargi pressing her questions. You read Patanjali defining yoga as the stilling of the turnings of the mind. You walked Valmiki's whole Ramayana, from a bird's cry to the earth opening. You kept a year of festivals. And this week, three paths: karma, bhakti, and jnana. Hindus don't all hear tat tvam asi the same way. Shankara's school hears it as one reality: you are Brahman. Ramanuja's hears the Lord living within you as your inner Self, inseparable from you, while you stay you. Both keep returning to this root. Year two was the root, and later teachers, and poets like Kamban and Tulsidas who retold Valmiki, keep coming back to it. Tomorrow, year three begins with the Mahabharata, and it opens not with a battle but with a king and a fire built for snakes.
screen: `AN ESSENCE TOO FINE TO SEE.` · `THE WHOLE BANYAN STANDS ON IT.` · `SALT, GARGI, PATANJALI, VALMIKI.` · `KARMA, BHAKTI, JNANA.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI: THAT YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: If there's a seed nearby, a peppercorn, a mustard seed, a grain of rice, hold it in your palm. Somewhere in it, Uddalaka would say, is a whole plant you can't see. Then let one line from year two rise on its own: that you are, the stilling of the mind, missing God is love, you are the tenth. Hold it on the breath, in on the first half, out on the second.
Mula. The root. The banyan stands on what you can't see, and later Hindu teachers keep returning to these roots: the Upanishads, Patanjali, Valmiki.
Keep this: tat tvam asi, that you are. The branches come next. Day six hundred ninety-six, and year two is done.

chat.meaning: Uddalaka showed Shvetaketu that the whole banyan stands on an essence too fine to see, the Self of all, and said: that you are. It's not 'be yourself'; it's that your deepest Self and everything's deepest reality aren't strangers.
